text: Every team building an internal developer platform makes the same mistake once: they instrument every application the platform deploys with careful dashboards, and leave the platform's own services — the CI runner fleet, the GitOps controller, the portal's backend — running on default logs and a shrug. That's backwards. If the GitOps controller stops syncing, nothing deploys anywhere, for anyone. The platform is the single most load-bearing production system in the organization.

Apply the same three pillars this course already used for applications, pointed at the platform itself. Metrics on the CI runner and GitOps controller. Structured logs for every sync attempt, job dispatch, and portal API request, so a failure traces back to a specific event instead of a gap in a graph. And distributed traces across the request path, so when a developer clicks 'create service,' you can see the whole fan-out, not just a vague feeling that something was slow.

On the CI runner, track queue depth, job wait time, job duration, failure rate, and concurrent jobs against capacity. On the GitOps controller — ArgoCD or Flux — track sync latency, the time between a commit and the cluster reconciling to match it, plus reconciliation error rate and how many applications currently sit out of sync or degraded. None of this is exotic; it's the same discipline you'd apply to any other production service.

Once you're collecting those numbers, write real service level objectives against them: ninety-five percent of CI jobs start within sixty seconds of being queued, ninety-nine percent of GitOps syncs complete within two minutes of a commit, portal API p95 latency stays under three hundred milliseconds. An SLO only matters if someone gets paged when it's at risk — which means the platform team needs its own on-call rotation and its own error budget.

A platform with no SLOs is informally promising infinite reliability to every team that depends on it, without ever saying so out loud. Instrumenting the platform's own services turns 'the CI system felt slow today' into an actual number you can act on, and it holds the platform team to the same standard it expects from everyone else — which is the only way 'platform as a product' means anything beyond a slogan.

You now have three layers of signal: DORA for delivery, SPACE for developer experience, and direct telemetry on the platform's own services. Next, we put all three together and use them to decide what the platform team actually builds next, instead of guessing.
